message.abstract: <jats:p>Medical-agent benchmarks commonly reduce an interactive execution to one terminal label. That reduction is useful for comparison, but it is insufficient for systems that change external state, must distinguish acknowledgment from commitment, and can improve across versions. This paper proposes an architecture-neutral evaluation protocol for evolvable medical agents. The protocol does not require RHIS or any other named controller. Participants may use any model, orchestration method, memory system, verification method, or external technology, and may improve their systems an unlimited number of times. The constraints apply to evidence and reporting rather than internal architecture: each formal task run must be executed autonomously by the participating AI system; first-pass results are immutable; every submitted version, failure, regression, cost, and handoff is retained; and official gold answers and scorer logic remain sealed from participants and may be used only for isolated post-run evaluation. The protocol separates four primary quantities: first-pass completion, later full-run completion, first-pass correctness, and later full-run correctness. It further separates official benchmark correctness from independently adjudicated real-world task correctness and governance correctness. Write tasks report transport acknowledgment, state confirmation, idempotency evidence, replay, partial mutation, atomicity, unresolved obligations, and human handoff. Cost reporting includes model calls, tokens, elapsed time, provider or infrastructure failure, and human review. A core contribution is the Principle of Contract Derivability: every scored obligation must be derivable from the visible task and tool contract even when test cases, expected values, and scorer implementation remain hidden. This principle prevents the benchmark from rewarding hidden-constraint guessing while preserving sealed answers and evaluation logic. The design is empirically motivated by the frozen 300-task RHIS MedAgentBench program reported in the preceding papers. That program completed 249 of 300 tasks on first pass, while known first-pass official correctness was 184 of 270 tasks because the 30-task Stage3D first-pass scorer result was unavailable. Later versions showed non-monotonic completion and correctness, scoped recovery that could not replace the first pass, acknowledged writes without proof of state commitment, and visible-contract answers rejected by hidden scoring. These observations do not establish clinical safety or RHIS superiority. They show why a benchmark for evolving action systems must preserve execution lineage, state evidence, contract visibility, and uncertainty instead of publishing only a best score. The paper concludes with a submission schema, clean-evaluation rules, metric definitions, and a strict public-repository boundary that excludes all RHIS controller information while permitting frozen RHIS results to remain an external comparator.</jats:p>
title: Benchmarking Evolvable Medical Agents Beyond First Pass
